state.case_summary:
A two-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of progressive, bilateral, painless swelling of the jaws over several months. On examination, he had symmetrical enlargement of the mandible and maxilla with intact, bluish-gray oral mucosa. Vital signs were normal, there was no lymphadenopathy, and routine hematologic tests were unremarkable. Panoramic radiography revealed well-defined, multilocular radiolucent areas involving the mandibular bodies, angles, ascending rami, and the maxillary tuberosities. Computed tomography of the jaws showed bilateral, expansile, multilocular lesions with thinning of the cortical plates of the maxilla and mandible, mild anterior displacement of an unerupted first molar, and no cortical breaches or soft-tissue extension.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. cherubism
B. Considered central giant
C. Considered hyperparathyroidism given giant
D. Considered Noonan/multiple giant cell lesion syndrome, but genetic testing distinguishes it
E. Considered Ramon syndrome, but it features “mental retardation, short stature, gingival fibromatosis, and epilepsy” not
F. Considered fibrous dysplasia, but that is “unilateral and does not show the swollen cheeks or upward turning of eyes
G. Considered Jaffe
H. Considered Neurofibromatosis type 1 among bone lesions, but the bilateral symmetry and posterior epicenter favor
